14	CASE OD2-HO-CONFOUND-1 (CONFOUND, organizational): Remote promotion gap at Fenwright Data Services
15	Setting: Fenwright Data Services is a fictional data-services company with about 1,100 employees across two offices, Larkhaven and Calderbrook, plus a fully remote workforce. Promotions are decided in one annual cycle: managers nominate and a Promotion Committee of directors approves or defers nominations. The FY2026 cycle closed in September 2026, and the People Analytics dashboard shows remote employees promoted at less than half the rate of office-based employees.
16	Presenting request: The COO has asked the People team to confirm by Friday that proximity bias explains the remote promotion gap, so the executive team can announce a rule that employees must work from an office at least three days a week to be considered for promotion. You have been asked to say what is driving the gap and what the company should do.
17	INITIAL EVIDENCE
18	E1 [stage S1] People Analytics promotion dashboard (system-record): Promotion dashboard, FY2026 cycle (census 31 Aug 2026; decisions effective 1 Oct 2026). Promotion rate = promotions divided by headcount at census. Office-based (including hybrid): 122 of 760 (16.1%). Remote: 26 of 340 (7.6%). By job family: Engineering, office 61/380 (16.1%), remote 14/170 (8.2%). Customer Operations, office 33/220 (15.0%), remote 7/110 (6.4%). Sales & Account Management, office 28/160 (17.5%), remote 5/60 (8.3%). Automated dashboard flag: 'Remote promotion rate below office rate in every job family.'
19	E2 [stage S1] Email from Danica Ferrol, Chief Operating Officer, to the executive team (leadership-account): Subject: Remote promotion gap. 'The dashboard could not be clearer. Remote staff are promoted at under half the office rate, in every job family. This is proximity bias, plain and simple: people who aren't in the room don't get seen. I propose that from the FY2027 cycle, anyone who wants to be considered for promotion works from an office at least three days a week. I know roughly 180 of our remote people live more than 150 km from Larkhaven or Calderbrook and were hired on home-based contracts, but if they want to progress they need to be visible. Can the People team confirm the diagnosis by Friday so we can announce?'
20	E3 [stage S1] HR business partner interview notes, 15 Oct 2026 (manager-account): Engineering manager (Larkhaven, team of 11, 5 remote): 'When an urgent client escalation comes in I'll usually hand it to whoever's sitting near me. It's quicker. I suppose that's the kind of work that gets noticed at promotion time.' Customer Operations manager (Calderbrook, team of 14, 6 remote): 'None of my remote people were put forward this year. Honestly, they're solid. Most of them haven't been with us long, and I didn't have a remote person I could make a case for yet.' Neither manager could say how many stretch assignments each team member had received this year.
21	E4 [stage S1] Fenwright Promotion Policy v4 (effective January 2024), section 3 (document): Section 3, Eligibility. 3.1 To be nominated in an annual cycle, an employee must have at least 18 months in their current level at the census date and a most recent performance rating of 'Meets' or above. 3.2 Managers nominate. The Promotion Committee approves or defers each nomination. 3.3 Exception nominations for employees with under 18 months in level require a director's written justification and are expected to be rare. 3.4 Work location is recorded on the nomination packet for administrative purposes.
22	E5 [stage S1] Engagement pulse survey, June 2026 (anonymous-staff-survey): Response rate: remote 71%, office-based 64%. 'I understand what I need to do to be promoted here': agree, remote 41%, office-based 58%. 'Senior leaders are aware of my work': agree, remote 33%, office-based 47%. 'My manager supports my career development': agree, remote 72%, office-based 70%. 'I have the tools I need to do my job well': agree, remote 81%, office-based 79%. Results are reported by work arrangement only; no breakdown by tenure is available in the survey tool.
23	CATALOGUE (full contents)
24	C1 [stage S1] Promotion nominations and outcomes by time in current level and work arrangement, FY2026 cycle - People Analytics extract from HRIS and promotion-workflow records (system-record): Census 31 Aug 2026. Eligible = 18+ months in current level. Office-based: eligible 560, nominated 160 (28.6%), approved 118 (73.8% of nominees; 21.1% of eligible). Not eligible 200, exception nominations 6, approved 4 (2.0%). Remote: eligible 110, nominated 31 (28.2%), approved 22 (71.0% of nominees; 20.0% of eligible). Not eligible 230, exception nominations 6, approved 4 (1.7%). Share of headcount eligible: office 73.7%, remote 32.4%. Applying office within-band rates to the remote eligibility mix gives an expected remote rate of 8.2%, against the observed 7.6%. Analyst note: the eligible-band difference of 1.1 points rests on 110 remote employees. It could be chance, and these data cannot rule out a true difference of several points in either direction.
25	C2 [stage S1] Hiring, transfer and voluntary exit records by work arrangement, January 2024 to August 2026 - HRIS workforce records (system-record): Remote hiring was opened to all roles in July 2024. Before that, remote work required an individual exception. Remote employees at 31 Aug 2026: 340. Start dates: before July 2024, 61; July 2024 to February 2025, 64; March 2025 to August 2026, 215. Office-based employees at 31 Aug 2026: 760, of whom 120 started in March 2025 or later. Voluntary exits in the 12 months to 31 Aug 2026: remote 31 (10.9% of average headcount 285); office-based 88 (11.6% of average headcount 757). First-year voluntary exit rate: remote 14.2%, office-based 15.0%. Transfers between arrangements since July 2024: 22 office-to-remote, 3 remote-to-office.
26	C3 [stage S1] Performance rating distribution by work arrangement, 2026 mid-year review - HRIS performance module (system-record): Five-point scale. Among rated employees: 'Meets' or above, remote 87%, office-based 88%. 'Exceeds' or above, remote 24%, office-based 27%. 'Below' or lower, remote 4%, office-based 3%. Employees with under six months' service at the review date are not rated: remote 92, office-based 41. Ratings are entered by line managers and moderated within each job family. No calibration adjustment by work arrangement was recorded.
27	C4 [stage S1] Promotion Committee calibration minutes, FY2026 cycle - Promotion Committee secretary (document): The committee of six directors met 9 to 11 September 2026 and reviewed 203 nominations, including 12 exception nominations. 148 were approved and 55 were not approved, 14 of them recorded as 'insufficient evidence of scope'. One director commented that 'remote cases tended to be thinner on cross-team examples'. The chair noted that this had not been checked.
28	C5 [stage S1] Promotion nomination form template and manager guidance, 2026 - People team intranet (document): The nomination form has four sections: scope evidence, impact examples, peer feedback and a readiness statement. The guidance asks managers to 'include at least two cross-team examples' and to keep the case under 1,200 words. Level, time in level, latest rating and work location are filled in automatically from HRIS. The guidance has not changed since the 2024 cycle apart from a new deadline date.
29	C6 [stage S1] Office badge-access records for office-based staff, January to August 2026 - Facilities access-control system (log): Office-based staff averaged 3.2 badge days per week (Larkhaven 3.4, Calderbrook 2.9). 14% of hybrid staff averaged fewer than one badge day per week. Attendance peaks on Tuesdays and Wednesdays. Records cover only employees assigned to an office and include no remote staff. The extract was not linked to promotion, rating or nomination data.
30	C7 [stage S1] Base-pay position within salary band by work arrangement, 2026 pay review - Reward team (financial-record): Median compa-ratio (base pay divided by band midpoint): remote 0.97, office-based 0.99. Under the offer guidelines, remote new hires since 2025 were placed at 0.95 on average. Pay is not location-adjusted within the country. The 2026 merit budget was 3.5% for both groups. The review found no band breaches and made no recommendations on work arrangement.
31	C8 [stage S1] Free-text comments from remote respondents, June 2026 engagement pulse - Survey vendor export (214 comments; selection shown) (anonymous-staff-survey): 'You have to be in Larkhaven to get noticed.' 'My manager is great but the directors have never met me.' 'Nobody told me when I was hired that I couldn't go for promotion until I'd been here a year and a half.' 'Office people get the fun client fires.' 'Remote has been fine for my career so far.' 'Visibility is a problem; I'm not sure promotions are.' The selection was chosen by the People team to illustrate themes and is not weighted by frequency.
32	C9 [stage S1] Interview with the Promotion Committee chair, 20 October 2026 - Director of Engineering (office-based), committee chair (leadership-account): 'We judge the case, not the postcode. Location is on the packet because payroll needs it, and nobody looks at it. If remote people aren't getting through, it's because they aren't being nominated, so talk to managers.' 33	C10 [stage S1] Industry report on promotion outcomes for remote workers, 2026 - Northgrid Insights, workplace-analytics vendor (external-data): Across 41 participating employers (anonymised), fully remote employees were promoted at 0.69 times the rate of office-based peers. The report attributes the gap to 'visibility deficits' and markets a visibility-coaching product. Methodology note: rates are raw promotions divided by headcount, with no adjustment for tenure, level or role. Participating employers self-selected, and Fenwright is not among them.
34	C11 [stage S1] Learning-platform course completions by work arrangement, January to August 2026 - Learning management system (telemetry): Average course completions per employee: remote 6.1, office-based 4.8. Mandatory compliance modules: 97% completion in both groups. Enrolment in the leadership-track programme: remote 9%, office-based 11%. Completion data are not linked to promotion records. The platform team notes that onboarding courses inflate completion counts for recent joiners.
35	C12 [stage S1] Reporting lines and manager span of control by work arrangement - HRIS organisation data (system-record): Of 340 remote employees, 221 (65%) report to office-based managers and 119 to remote managers. Average span of control: office-based managers 8.1 direct reports, remote managers 7.6. Average number of manager changes in the past 12 months: remote 0.3, office-based 0.3. This extract does not include promotion, nomination or rating outcomes by manager location.
36	C13 [stage S1] Project staffing records by work arrangement, January to August 2026 - Project staffing system export (system-record): Records project codes and hours booked per employee. Average concurrent projects: remote 2.3, office-based 2.4. The 'role on project' field, intended to flag lead or stretch roles, is blank on 71% of records. Client-escalation work is booked to a general support code and is not attributed to individuals. People Analytics comment: 'This system cannot tell us who received stretch or high-visibility work.'
37	C14 [stage S1] FY2025 promotion cycle summary by work arrangement - People Analytics annual report, October 2025 (prior-report): FY2025 cycle, census 31 Aug 2025. Promotion rate = promotions divided by headcount at census. Office-based: 113 of 731 (15.5%). Remote: 17 of 181 (9.4%). The report comments that 'the remote gap warrants attention' and recommends that leadership 'monitor visibility'. No breakdown by level, tenure or job family was produced, and no follow-up analysis was commissioned.
38	C15 [stage S1] Office space utilisation report, Larkhaven and Calderbrook, 2026 - Facilities management (document): Larkhaven: 520 desks, average daily occupancy 61%, peak 84% on Wednesdays. Calderbrook: 300 desks, average daily occupancy 55%, peak 77%. The report estimates that an extra 180 regular attenders at three days a week could be absorbed at Larkhaven only by reintroducing desk booking. The Calderbrook lease renewal is due in 2027.
39	CANDIDATES
40	H1: The remote–office promotion gap arises because managers and the Promotion Committee favour employees they work alongside in person.
41	H2: The remote–office promotion gap arises because remote employees, as a group, have spent less time in their current level than office-based employees, not because of where they work.
42	H3: The remote–office promotion gap arises because remote employees are concentrated in job families that offer fewer promotions.
43	H4: Remote employees are offered fewer stretch or high-visibility assignments than comparable office-based employees.
44	H5: The remote–office promotion gap arises because remote employees leave the company at a higher rate, so fewer of them stay long enough to be considered for promotion.
45	R1: Employee works remotely -> Lower chance of promotion in the FY2026 cycle (causes)
46	R2: Fewer months in current level at the census date -> Lower chance of promotion in the FY2026 cycle (causes)
47	R3: Employee works remotely -> Higher voluntary attrition (causes)
48	A1: Adopt the COO's proposal: from the FY2027 cycle, require at least three office days a week for any employee to be considered for promotion.
49	A2: Put the attendance proposal on hold, and change promotion reporting to compare remote and office-based employees who were eligible under the policy, then re-check that comparison at the FY2027 cycle.
50	A3: Replace manager-assigned stretch work with a centrally posted, application-based process to correct remote employees' reduced access to it.
51	A4: Run briefings for remote employees that explain the promotion criteria and eligibility rules.
52	SCORED ITEMS

54	Q2: hypothesis H2 allowed=[supported, contradicted, unknown]
55	Q3: hypothesis H3 allowed=[supported, contradicted, unknown]
56	Q4: hypothesis H4 allowed=[supported, contradicted, unknown]
57	Q5: hypothesis H5 allowed=[supported, contradicted, unknown]
58	Q6: edge R1 allowed=[causal, association-only, contradicted, unknown]
59	Q7: edge R2 allowed=[causal, association-only, contradicted, unknown]
60	Q8: edge R3 allowed=[causal, association-only, contradicted, unknown]
61	Q9: action A1 allowed=[preferred, acceptable, premature, harmful]
62	Q10: action A2 allowed=[preferred, acceptable, premature, harmful]
63	Q11: action A3 allowed=[preferred, acceptable, premature, harmful]
64	Q12: action A4 allowed=[preferred, acceptable, premature, harmful]
65	Q13: sufficiency SUFF allowed=[sufficient, insufficient]

answers.justification: Among eligible employees, nomination rates (28.6% vs 28.2%) and committee approval rates (73.8% vs 71.0%) are almost the same, and adjusting for eligibility mix predicts a remote rate of 8.2% against 7.6% observed (C1), so in-person favouritism does not explain the gap; E3, C4 and C9 are anecdotal or untallied.

Only 32.4% of remote employees meet the 18-month time-in-level rule, against 73.7% of office staff (C1, E4 3.1), because 215 of 340 remote staff joined after remote hiring opened (C2); applying office rates within each band reproduces nearly all of the gap (C1).
Remote and office staff are spread across job families in similar proportions (about 50/32/18% vs 50/29/21%), and the gap appears inside every family (E1).
The only support is one manager's anecdote (E3) and selected comments (C8); the staffing system cannot show who received stretch or escalation work (C13), and the managers could not count it (E3).
Remote voluntary exit rates are slightly lower than office rates, both overall (10.9% vs 11.6%) and in the first year (14.2% vs 15.0%) (C2).

The raw gap is real (E1, C14), but almost all of it disappears once eligibility is controlled for (C1), and the analyst note says a residual effect of a few points can be neither confirmed nor ruled out, so causation is not established.

Policy 3.1 bars nomination under 18 months in level except by rare exception (E4), which gives the mechanism, and approval rates are about 2% for ineligible staff against about 21% for eligible staff in both groups (C1).
Remote attrition is not higher than office attrition, overall or in the first year (C2).

The rule targets a cause the data do not support (C1). It would effectively shut out about 180 remote staff on home-based contracts from promotion (E2), likely punishing the wrong group, and Larkhaven lacks the desk capacity without reintroducing booking (C15).

The gap comes from comparing headcounts with very different eligibility (E1, C1, C14), so pausing A1 and reporting eligible-to-eligible comparisons, then re-checking the uncertain residual next cycle (C1 analyst note), fits the evidence.
There is no data showing remote staff get less stretch work (C13), so H4 is unconfirmed (E3, C8 are anecdotal) and a structural overhaul is not yet justified.

Remote staff understand promotion criteria less (41% vs 58%, E5), and comments show some did not know about the 18-month rule (C8), so briefings are low-risk and helpful, but they do not address the main reporting error.
C1 (consistent with C2 and E4) is strong enough to decide not to adopt the attendance rule and to fix the reporting, even though a small residual effect remains uncertain.

C3 is mildly off-topic, since unrated recent joiners cannot meet E4's rating requirement, but it is consistent with the tenure explanation.
